p.src: Now Pigsy had been seized by a troop of monkeys, who carried, hoisted, tugged, and dragged him until they tore his cassock. He grumbled on and on, muttering to himself, “It is all over, all over! This time I am in for a fatal beating.” Before long they reached the cave entrance. The Great Sage sat atop a rocky ledge and cursed him: “You bran-stuffed oaf! Leaving was bad enough—why did you curse me?” Bajie knelt on the ground and said, “Brother, I never cursed you. If I did, may I chew my own tongue out. I only said that since you would not come, I would go back and report to Master myself. How would I dare curse you?” The Pilgrim said, “How could you ever deceive me? When I tug my left ear upward, I can hear what people in the Thirty-three Heavens are saying; when I tug my right ear downward, I can hear the Ten Kings of Hell reckoning accounts with their judges. You cursed me as you walked away—how could I not hear?” Bajie said, “Brother, I knew how sly and furtive you are. You must have changed into something again and followed me to listen.” The Pilgrim cried, “Little ones, choose stout cudgels! First give him twenty blows on the shins by way of greeting, then twenty across his back; afterward I shall see him off with my iron staff.” Terrified, Bajie kowtowed and said, “Brother, for Master’s sake, please spare me!” The Pilgrim said, “A fine man of benevolence and honor that master is!” Bajie said again, “Brother, if you will not do it for Master, then for the sake of the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea, please spare me.”

p.src: At the mention of the Bodhisattva, the Pilgrim relented somewhat and said, “Brother, since you put it that way, I shall not beat you for now. But tell me the truth and hide nothing. What trouble has the Tang Monk met with that made you come here to deceive me?” Bajie said, “Brother, there is no great trouble. He truly misses you.” The Pilgrim cursed him: “You wretched creature begging for a beating! Why are you still trying to fool me? Though old Sun’s body has returned to the Water Curtain Cave, his heart follows the scripture-seeking monk. That master meets trouble at every step and calamity wherever he goes. Tell me at once, and you will escape a beating.” Hearing this, Bajie kowtowed and confessed, “Brother, I did mean to conceal it from you so that I could persuade you to come. I never expected you to be so perceptive. Spare me the beating, let me rise, and I shall tell you.” The Pilgrim said, “Very well. Get up and speak.” The monkeys released him. The fool sprang up and glanced wildly to either side. The Pilgrim said, “What are you looking for?” Bajie said, “I am seeing which path is open enough to run along.” The Pilgrim said, “Where could you run? Even if I gave you a three-day head start, old Sun has the means to chase you down and bring you back. Speak quickly! Once you provoke my temper, I shall never spare you.”

p.src: Bajie said, “To tell you the truth, brother, after you returned here, Sandy and I escorted Master onward. We came to a black pine forest, where Master dismounted and sent me to beg for food. I went a great distance without finding a single household. Weary from the effort, I lay down in the grass for a short sleep. Unexpectedly, Sandy left Master and came looking for me. You know Master cannot sit still; he went walking alone through the forest to admire the scenery. On leaving the forest, he saw a golden pagoda shining with light and took it for a monastery. But beneath the pagoda was a fiend called Yellow Robe, who captured him. When Sandy and I returned to look for him, we found only the white horse and the luggage; Master was gone. We followed the trail to the cave entrance and fought the monster. Master was inside the cave, and fortunately he found a savior. It was none other than the third princess of the King of Baoxiang, whom the monster had abducted. She wrote a letter home and entrusted Master to deliver it. Then, on some pretext, she persuaded the monster to release him. When we reached the kingdom and delivered the letter, the king asked Master to subdue the fiend and bring back the princess. Brother, you know him—could that old monk possibly subdue a fiend? The two of us went to fight again, but we did not realize how immense the monster’s magic was, and he captured Sandy too. Defeated, I fled and hid in the grass. The monster changed into a handsome scholar, entered the royal court, and claimed kinship with the king; then he transformed Master into a tiger. Then the White Dragon Horse came to the rescue. At night he assumed his dragon form and went looking for Master. He failed to find him, but came upon the monster drinking in the Silver Peace Hall. He changed into a palace maid, poured wine for the monster, and danced with a sword, hoping to seize a chance to cut him down. Instead, the monster struck him with his Full Hall Red weapon and injured his leg. It was he who told me to come and ask you, saying, ‘Elder Brother is a righteous and benevolent gentleman. A gentleman does not dwell on past wrongs, so he will surely come and save Master from this peril.’ Brother, I implore you to remember that ‘a teacher for one day is a father for life’ and save him, whatever it takes.”

p.src: The Pilgrim said, “You fool! When I left, I charged you again and again, saying, ‘If some demon captures Master, tell it that old Sun is his chief disciple.’ Why did you not mention me?” Bajie thought again, “A challenge will work better than an invitation. Let me provoke him.” He said, “Brother, it would have been better if I had not mentioned you. It was because I did that he became even more outrageous.” The Pilgrim said, “What did you say?” Bajie said, “I told him, ‘Fiend, do not be insolent or harm my master. I have an elder brother named Sun the Pilgrim, whose magic powers are immense and who excels at subduing demons. When he comes, he will leave you without a place to be buried.’ On hearing this, the monster grew still more furious and cursed, ‘What sort of creature is this Sun the Pilgrim? Do you think I fear him? If he comes, I shall skin him, tear out his sinews, gnaw his bones, and eat his heart. Scrawny though that monkey may be, I shall still chop him into pickled mince and fry him in oil.’” At this, the Pilgrim was so enraged that he scratched his ears and cheeks and leapt about furiously, crying, “Who dares curse me like that?” Bajie said, “Calm your anger, brother. It was the Yellow-Robed Monster who cursed you so. I merely repeated his words for you to hear.” The Pilgrim said, “Worthy brother, rise. It is not that I cannot go. Since the fiend has dared curse me, I cannot leave him unsubdued. I shall go with you. Five hundred years ago, old Sun caused havoc in Heaven. Whenever the divine generals beneath the sky saw me, every one of them bent his back, bowed low, and addressed me as Great Sage. This monster is insolent enough to curse me behind my back. I shall go, seize him, and tear him into ten thousand pieces to avenge his insults! Once I have taken my revenge, I shall return at once.” Bajie said, “Exactly so, brother. You need only go and capture the fiend and avenge yourself. After that, whether you come with us or not is entirely up to you.”

p.src: Only then did the Great Sage leap down from the cliff, rush into the cave, and take off his demon disguise. He straightened his brocade robe, tightened his tiger-skin kilt, took up his iron staff, and strode straight out through the gate. The troop of monkeys hurriedly barred his way and cried, “Grandfather Great Sage, where are you going? Stay and lead us in our games for a few years at least.” The Pilgrim said, “Little ones, what are you saying? As for my duty of protecting the Tang Monk, all in Heaven and on earth know that Sun Wukong is his disciple. He did not really drive me away; he merely told me to visit home and sent me back to enjoy myself at ease. Now, however, this affair has arisen. You must all guard our estate with care, planting willows and pines at the proper seasons, and never let it fall into neglect. Let me return to protect the Tang Monk. Once we have brought the scriptures back to the Eastern Land and accomplished our work, I shall return and share the joys of our natural life with you.” The monkeys each accepted his command.

p.src: The Great Sage and Bajie then joined hands and rode a cloud away from the cave. After crossing the Eastern Ocean and reaching its western shore, they halted their radiant cloud, and he said, “Brother, go slowly here while I descend into the sea and wash myself clean.” Bajie said, “We are hurrying on our journey. Why stop to wash yourself?” The Pilgrim said, “What would you know about it? Since returning home, I have picked up something of a demonic smell these past few days. Master is fastidious about cleanliness, and I fear he may take offense.” Only then did Bajie understand that the Pilgrim was utterly sincere and harbored no other intention.

p.src: In a short while he finished washing, and they mounted the cloud again and continued westward, until they saw the golden pagoda shining. Bajie pointed and said, “Is that not the Yellow-Robed Monster’s home? Brother Sha is still inside.” The Pilgrim said, “Remain in the air while I go down and see how matters stand before the gate, so that I may meet the monster in battle.” Bajie said, “Do not go. The monster is not at home.” The Pilgrim said, “I know.” That splendid Monkey King lowered his auspicious cloud and went straight to inspect the cave entrance. There he saw two little boys playing with curved sticks, striking a feathered ball and competing for the goal. One was about ten years old, and the other eight or nine. While they were absorbed in their game, the Pilgrim rushed up. Caring nothing whose children they might be, he seized each by his topknot and hauled them over. The frightened children screamed wildly, weeping and hurling abuse. Their cries alarmed the lesser demons of the Moon-Wave Cave, who hurried to report to the princess, “Madam, someone we do not know has carried off the two young masters!” The two children were, in fact, the offspring of the princess and the monster.

p.src: Hearing this, the princess hurried out of the cave and saw the Pilgrim standing atop the high cliff, holding the two children as though about to dash them down. In alarm, the princess shouted sternly, “You there! I have no quarrel with you. Why have you seized my sons? Their father is formidable. If anything happens to them, he will never let you be.” The Pilgrim said, “Do you not recognize me? I am Sun Wukong the Pilgrim, the Tang Monk’s senior disciple. My junior fellow-disciple, Monk Sha, is inside your cave. Go and release him, and I shall return these two children to you. Two exchanged for one—you will still have the better bargain.” When the princess heard this, she hurried inside, ordered the gate-guarding demons away, and personally untied Monk Sha. Monk Sha said, “Princess, do not release me. I fear that when your monster returns, he will demand his prisoner and cause you to suffer his anger.” The princess said, “Reverend sir, you are my benefactor. You delivered my family letter and spoke in my defense, saving my life, so I too have been watching for a chance to release you. Unexpectedly, your senior fellow-disciple Sun Wukong has come to the cave entrance and is demanding that I set you free.”

p.src: Now Bajie, who had remained suspended in the air, saw Monk Sha emerge from the cave and immediately lowered his cloud, calling, “Brother Sha, bear up! Bear up!” Seeing him, Monk Sha said, “Second Brother, where have you come from?” Bajie said, “After losing yesterday’s battle, I entered the city at night and met the white horse. I learned that Master was in trouble: Yellow Robe had used magic to turn him into a tiger. The white horse and I discussed it, and I went to invite our senior brother.” The Pilgrim said, “Idiot, enough of your reunion talk. Each of you take one of these children in your arms. Go first into the city of Baoxiang and provoke the monster into coming here, where I shall wait to fight him.” Monk Sha said, “Brother, how are we to provoke him?” The Pilgrim said, “You two are to mount your clouds and stand above the Golden Throne Hall. Without worrying about right or wrong, dash the children down before the white jade steps. If anyone asks who you are, say that these are the sons of the Yellow-Robed Monster and that the two of you captured and brought them there. Once the monster hears of it, he is certain to return, and I shall have no need to enter the city to fight him. If we fought over the city, we would surely spew clouds and belch mist, scattering earth and raising dust. The court, its many officials, and the common people would all be alarmed and disturbed.” Bajie laughed and said, “Brother, whenever you undertake something, you always leave us holding the wrong end of it.” The Pilgrim said, “How have I wronged you?” Bajie said, “These two children were already frightened out of their wits when you seized them. By now they have cried themselves hoarse, and before long they will surely die. If we take them and dash them down until they become lumps of mangled flesh, will the monster let us go when he catches up? He will certainly demand our two lives in repayment. Meanwhile, will you not remain entirely blameless? There will not even be a witness to connect you with it. Is that not leaving us in the wrong?” The Pilgrim said, “If he grabs at you, the two of you are to fight him and draw him back here. The battlefield here is broad. I shall wait for him and fight him here.” Monk Sha said, “Exactly, exactly. Eldest Brother is right. Let us go.” Only then did the two of them, relying on their martial might, carry the children away.

p.src: Wukong immediately leapt down from the rocky cliff and came beneath the gate of the tower. The princess said, “You monk have no sense of honor at all! You said that if I released your junior brother, you would give me my children. Why did you let your junior brother go, keep my children behind, and then come back to my door?” Wukong answered with an ingratiating smile, “Do not be angry, Princess. You have been away a long time, so I have taken your sons to meet their maternal grandfather.” The princess said, “Do not be insolent, monk. My Yellow-Robed Lord is unlike ordinary men. If you have frightened my children and given him a nasty shock, see what will become of you.” Wukong laughed and said, “Princess, when a person lives between Heaven and Earth, what constitutes the gravest offense?” The princess said, “I know.” Wukong said, “What could a woman like you know?” The princess said, “I was raised in the palace and instructed by my parents from childhood. I remember an ancient book saying, ‘The offenses punishable by the Five Penalties number three thousand, yet none is greater than being unfilial.’” Wukong said, “Then you are precisely an unfilial person. For it is said, ‘My father begot me; my mother nurtured me. Alas, my parents! What toil they endured in giving me life!’ Thus filial piety is the source of all conduct and the foundation of every virtue. How, then, could you give yourself to a demon and cease even to think of your parents? If that is not the offense of being unfilial, what is?” Hearing these righteous words, the princess’s ears reddened and her face flushed for a long while, and she was overwhelmed with shame. At last she blurted out, “Your words are most just, venerable sir. How could I not miss my parents? It is only because this demon abducted and deceived me into coming here. p.src: The demon leaped about in fury and cried, “It is over, it is over! He dashed my son to death, and there is no bringing him back. All I can do is seize that monk and make him pay for my son’s life. Wife, weep no more. How do you feel now? Let me treat you first.” The Pilgrim said, “Nothing much is wrong. I simply cannot bear the loss of our child, and crying has made my heart ache.” The demon said, “That is nothing serious. Get up. I have a treasure here; one rub over the painful spot and it will cease to hurt. But take great care not to flick it with your thumb; for if your thumb should flick it, my true form will be revealed.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim laughed inwardly. “This wretched monster is remarkably honest: without any torture, he has confessed everything himself. When he brings out the treasure, I shall give it a flick and see what kind of monster he is.” The monster took the Pilgrim by the hand and led him straight into a remote, tightly sealed recess deep within the cave. Then he spat a treasure from his mouth, about the size of a hen’s egg: an exquisite inner elixir, a śarīra pearl. The Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly. “What a fine thing! Who knows how many sessions of meditation, how many years of trial, and how many cycles of matching yin and yang it took to refine this inner-elixir śarīra? Today it has had the great good fortune to meet old Sun.” The monkey took it. Though he had no pain anywhere, he deliberately rubbed it over himself, then flicked it away with one finger. The demon panicked and snatched at it. But consider how nimble that monkey was: he sucked the treasure straight into his belly. The demon clenched his fist and struck at him. The Pilgrim blocked the blow with one hand, wiped his face, and revealed his true form. “Monster,” he cried, “show some manners! Take a good look and see who I am!”

When I captured the Tang Monk, I knew only that he had two disciples named Zhu Bajie and Friar Sand. When did anyone ever mention a fellow surnamed Sun? You must be some creature from who knows where, come here to deceive me.” The Pilgrim said, “I did not come with those two. Because old Sun habitually fought monsters and had killed and wounded so many, my master, being compassionate and devoted to goodness, expelled me and sent me home. That is why I did not travel with them. You simply did not know your ancestor’s name.” The monster said, “What a spineless fellow you are! Having been driven away by your master, how can you still have the face to appear before anyone?” The Pilgrim said, “You wretched monster, what do you know of the saying, ‘A teacher for one day is a father for life’? Or ‘No quarrel between father and son lasts overnight’? You have harmed my master; how could I fail to come and rescue him? Was harming him not enough? Why did you also abuse me behind my back?” The monster said, “When did I ever abuse you?” The Pilgrim said, “Zhu Bajie told me so.” The monster said, “Do not believe him. That sharp-snouted Zhu Bajie is rather fond of wagging his tongue like a gossiping old woman. Why listen to him?” The Pilgrim said, “There is no need to discuss such idle talk. Let us speak only of how, now that old Sun has come to your home, you have been a poor host to a guest from afar. Though you have no wine or food to offer, at least you have a head. Quickly stretch it over here, and let old Sun serve you one blow in place of tea.” Hearing talk of fighting, the monster laughed aloud. “Pilgrim Sun, you have miscalculated. Since you intended to fight, you should not have followed me inside. There are still a hundred or so demons here, great and small. Even if your whole body were covered in hands, you could not fight your way out of my gate.” The Pilgrim said, “Do not talk nonsense. Never mind a hundred—even if there were thousands or tens of thousands, so long as I could count them clearly one by one, every stroke of my staff would find its mark, and I would root you out without a trace.”

p.src: At this, the Great Sage could no longer contain his anger. Gripping his iron staff, he turned a somersault and leapt straight to the Southern Gate of Heaven. Pang, Liu, Gou, Bi, Zhang, Tao, Deng, Xin, and the others were so alarmed that they bowed on either side, bent-backed and deferential. Not daring to bar his way, they let him charge through the heavenly gate and proceed directly to the Hall of Radiant Light. The four great Celestial Masters Zhang, Ge, Xu, and Qiu were already there and asked, “What brings you here, Great Sage?” The Pilgrim replied, “While escorting the Tang Monk to the Kingdom of Precious Image, I encountered a fiend who had deceived the king’s daughter and harmed my master, so Old Sun fought him. Right in the midst of the battle, the creature disappeared. I reckoned that it was no earthly monster but most likely some spirit from Heaven, so I have come expressly to investigate which divine being has left his appointed station.” On hearing this, the Celestial Masters immediately entered the Hall of Miraculous Mist and reported the matter. They received orders to inspect the officers of the Nine Luminaries, the Twelve Zodiacal Spirits, the Five Dippers of the east, west, south, north, and center, the hosts of stars in the Milky Way, the gods of the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers, and every holy being under Heaven. All were present in Heaven, and not one had dared leave his appointed station. u.src: At this, the Great Sage could no longer contain his anger. Gripping his iron staff, he turned a somersault and leapt straight to the Southern Gate of Heaven.

Right in the midst of the battle, the creature disappeared.
I reckoned that it was no earthly monster but most likely some spirit from Heaven, so I have come expressly to investigate which divine being has left his appointed station.”
On hearing this, the Celestial Masters immediately entered the Hall of Miraculous Mist and reported the matter.

p.src: The officers of the other twenty-seven lodges received the decree, passed through the heavenly gate, and each recited an incantation, startling the Kui Star from hiding. And where, you may ask, had he been hiding? He was in fact a divine general whom the Great Sage Sun had beaten into terror during his havoc in Heaven. He had slipped into a mountain ravine to lie low until the danger passed, and the watery vapors concealed his demonic cloud, which was why he had not been seen. Only when he heard the officers of his own division reciting their spells did he dare show himself, and he followed them back to Heaven. The Great Sage blocked him at the heavenly gate and was about to strike, but fortunately the other stars restrained him and escorted the culprit before the Jade Emperor. The monster took a golden tablet from his belt and kowtowed below the throne, confessing his guilt. The Jade Emperor said, “Kui Wood Wolf, Heaven offers boundless delights, yet instead of enjoying them you secretly fled elsewhere. Why?” The Kui Lodge kowtowed and memorialized, “Your Majesty, spare your servant from death. The princess of the King of Precious Image was no mortal. She was originally the Jade Maiden who tended incense in the Incense Hall. She desired a secret union with me, but I feared defiling the sacred precincts of Heaven. Longing for mortal life, she descended first and was reborn within the imperial palace. Unwilling to betray our former pledge, I transformed myself into a monster, occupied a famous mountain, carried her off to my cave, and lived with her as husband and wife for thirteen years. ‘Every sip and every bite is surely ordained beforehand.’ Now the Great Sage Sun has come, and the affair has reached its conclusion.” When the Jade Emperor heard this, he confiscated the golden tablet and demoted Kui to the Tushita Palace to tend the furnaces for the Supreme Lord Lao. He was to retain his salary while serving this penal duty: if he earned merit, he would be restored to office; if not, his punishment would be increased.

p.src: The princess heard only the rush of wind in her ears, and in an instant she was back inside the city. The three disciples brought her into the Golden Throne Hall. The princess bowed reverently to her royal father and mother and was reunited with her sisters. All the officials came to pay their respects. Only then did the princess report, “Thanks to Elder Sun’s boundless magic power, the Yellow-Robed Monster was subdued and your daughter was rescued and brought home.” The king asked, “What sort of creature was Yellow Robe?” The Pilgrim replied, “Your Majesty’s son-in-law was the Kui Star of the upper realm, while your beloved daughter was the Jade Maiden who tended incense and descended to the mortal world because she longed for earthly life. This was no trifling matter: it all arose from affinities and obligations formed in a previous existence, which destined them for this marriage. Old Sun went to the Celestial Palace and reported the monster to the Jade Emperor. The Emperor discovered that he had missed four musters. His thirteen days in the lower world amounted to thirteen years. —For one day in Heaven is one year in the lower world. —The Jade Emperor then sent the stars of his own division to bring him back to Heaven and demoted him to the Tushita Palace, there to earn merit. And Old Sun has rescued your beloved daughter and brought her back.” The king thanked the Pilgrim for his great kindness and ordered, “Now go and see to your master.”

p.src: The three disciples descended directly from the throne hall and went with the officials to the court offices. They carried out the iron cage and removed the iron chains from the false tiger. Everyone else saw a tiger, but the Pilgrim alone saw a man. The truth was that the master had been oppressed by the monster’s spell. He could not move, and though his mind was clear, he could open neither mouth nor eyes. The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Master, what a fine monk you are! How did you manage to take on such an ugly appearance? You accused me of violence and wickedness and drove me away, while you meant to devote yourself wholly to goodness. How, then, did you suddenly acquire such a face?” Bajie said, “Brother, just save him now. Stop exposing his faults.” The Pilgrim said, “You are always the one egging him on, and you are his favored and faithful disciple. If you would not save him, why did you come seeking Old Sun? I told you from the outset that once I had subdued the monster and avenged his abuse of me, I would go back.” Sha Monk stepped forward, knelt, and said, “Brother, the ancients said, ‘If you have no regard for the monk, at least have regard for the Buddha.’ Since you have come this far, elder brother, we earnestly beg you to save him. If we had been able to save him ourselves, we would never have dared travel so far to ask you to come.” The Pilgrim took him by the hand and raised him, saying, “How could I possibly have resolved not to save him? Quickly, fetch some water.” Bajie sped back to the posthouse, collected the baggage and horses, took out the purple-gold alms bowl, filled it halfway with water, and handed it to the Pilgrim. The Pilgrim took the water, recited a true incantation, and spat a mouthful straight onto the tiger’s head. The sorcery receded, and the aura of the tiger dissolved.

p.src: The elder regained his original form. After composing himself and opening his eyes, he recognized the Pilgrim. He seized him by the arm and said, “Wukong, where have you come from?” Standing beside them, Sha Monk related the whole story in detail: how they had invited the Pilgrim back, subdued the monster, rescued the princess, dispelled the tiger’s aura, and returned to court. Sanzang thanked him over and over, saying, “Worthy disciple, it is all thanks to you—truly, all thanks to you. When this journey is done, we shall soon reach the Western Heaven, then return directly to the Eastern Land and report to the Tang emperor that your merit stands foremost.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Say no more, say no more.
